newsitem.title: UGANDA: Swiss firm seeks to join Uganda coffee bid.
newsitem.headline: Swiss firm seeks to join Uganda coffee bid.

text.p: Swiss company Sucafina, whose sole bid to purchase a 51 percent shareholding in the Uganda's Coffee Marketing Board Limited (CMBL) was rejected by the Ugandan government in December, has formally asked to join a new bid by a local consortium.
On Thursday, the government placed advertisements in Kampala newspapers asking for fresh bids for the stake. It said bidding would close at 1330 GMT and bids would be opened at 1400 GMT on May 9.
Jamada Lutta Musoke, chairman of the UGACAP (Uganda Consortium of Agro-Processors) consortium involved in the bid, told Reuters on Thursday that Sucafina's Ugandan partner, UGACOF, had asked to join.
UGACOF Managing Director Ignacio Gomez asked on April 3 to join Musoke's group, which includes leading players Zigoti, Kyagalanyi, Nzamba Coffee Works and Busiro, Musoke said.
The government called for fresh bids for 51 percent of its shareholding in the CMBL on Tuesday.
In a report dated April 1, CMBL privatisation coordinator William Okecho had said talks to get Sucafina to raise an original bid of $3.3 million had failed.
On March 19, a consortium of five Ugandan companies had urged the government to re-open bidding for the CMBL, but at the time Minister Rukikaire said such a move would be unfair.
UGACAP has placed a bid of $5.5 million.
"Sucafina is free to join us provided they meet our requirements...We now have 15 companies and are moving to 20," Musoke said.
He would not discuss the obligations for each member or whether the consortium would now raise its bid in view of wider participation by local companies and Sucafina interest.
Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA) executives have said a bid of around $10 million would be acceptable.

Previously, Ugandan privatisation officials have said that a bidder who offered two-thirds of the value price would be considered serious but if one was not found then they would be comfortable selling at a lower price only to Ugandan investors.
CMBL privatisation coordinator William Okecho said the consortium must tranform itself into a company to qualify to tender. Musoke would not say when that would happen.

CMBL assets included in the sale were valued at $36.7 million. The company's principal asset is its processing and storage unit in Bugoolobi. It has an export processing capacity of four million 60-kg bags a year.
CMBL's share of the coffee export business fell to 9.4 percent in 1995 from o around 84 percent four years earlier. Uganda has more than 100 private coffee exporters.
